identity.title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Training Dynamics for Language Model Reasoning

problem.claim: Downstream developers need to evaluate how training-stage design choices affect language models, but multi-stage training makes this difficult.

contributions.claim: EvoLM enables systematic and transparent analysis of training dynamics across pre-training, continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
The authors train over 100 1B- and 4B-parameter language models to study upstream and downstream reasoning, including in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.
The authors release models, stage-specific training datasets, and the complete training and evaluation pipeline.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish EvoLM as a model suite for systematic and transparent cross-stage analysis of language-model training dynamics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report diminishing returns from excessive pre-training and post-training.
The authors report that mitigating forgetting matters during domain-specific continued pre-training and that continued pre-training helps bridge pre-training and post-training.
The authors report intricate trade-offs in configuring supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-stage LM training complicates evaluation of stage-specific design choices.
EvoLM is introduced as a transparent suite for analyzing dynamics across four training stages.
More than 100 1B- and 4B-parameter models are trained from scratch and evaluated on upstream, downstream, in-domain, and out-of-domain reasoning.
The study reports stage-specific trade-offs and releases models, datasets, and the full pipeline for open research and reproducibility.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links stage-specific training choices to both upstream and downstream reasoning, while explicitly distinguishing in-domain from out-of-domain generalization.

lessons.interpretation: Separating capability levels and generalization regimes can make training-dynamics claims more diagnostically useful.
lessons.application: When presenting a training intervention, report its effects separately on modeling, task reasoning, and in-domain versus out-of-domain tests.
lessons.exception: This decomposition may be unsuitable when the study targets only one capability or has no meaningful domain shift.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative results, evaluation-task details, or precise training configurations.
The reported trade-offs and forgetting-mitigation practices are not specified in enough detail to reproduce from the abstract alone.
